original_value: SummaryBug‐assignment (BA), the task of ranking developers in terms of the relevance of their expertise to fix a new bug report is time consuming, which is why substantial attention has been paid to developing methods for automating it. In this article, we describe a new BA approach that relies on two key intuitions. Similar to traditional BA methods, our method constructs the expertise profile of project developers, based on the textual elements of the bugs they have fixed in the past; unlike traditional methods, however, our method considers only the programming keywords in these bug descriptions, relying on Stack Overflow as the vocabulary for these keywords. The second key intuition of our method is that recent expertise is more relevant than past expertise, which is why our method weighs the relevance of a developer's expertise based on how recently they have fixed a bug with keywords similar to the bug at hand. We evaluated our BA method using a dataset of 93k bug‐report assignments from 13 popular GitHub projects. In spite of its simplicity, our method predicts the assignee with high accuracy, outperforming state‐of‐the‐art methods.

result.paraphrase: Summary Bug assignment (BA), ranking developers by how relevant their expertise is for fixing a new bug report, is time-consuming, which is why much effort has gone into automating it. In this article, we present a new BA approach built on two main intuitions. Like traditional BA methods, our approach builds expertise profiles for project developers from the textual elements of bugs they have fixed before; unlike conventional methods, it uses only the programming keywords in those bug descriptions and takes Stack Overflow as the vocabulary for those keywords. Its second intuition is that recent expertise matters more than older expertise, so the method weights a developer’s expertise by how recently they fixed a bug with keywords similar to the current one. We evaluated the BA method on 93k bug-report assignments from 13 popular GitHub projects. Despite its simplicity, it predicts the assignee with high accuracy and outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
